$comment: How the brain reads a visual as one thing: what the research says about COMBINING components (shape, colour, type, layout, motion, imagery), not about each one alone. Every finding here feeds a rule in foundations/combinations/combinations.json, which the composer (npm run compose) applies once per product or campaign, so designs start from a researched combination instead of trial and error. Sources were checked against their published abstracts (2026-10-09); where a number could not be confirmed it is not used.

findings.claim: People rate shapes, colours, typefaces, words and motion on the same few affective dimensions: evaluation (good-bad), potency (strong-weak) and activity (active-passive).
findings.use: Every component in the guide is placed on the same axes, so they can be compared and matched: roundness, activity, potency, warmth, hand.
sources: Osgood, Suci & Tannenbaum (1957), The Measurement of Meaning
Doyle & Bottomley (2006), Journal of Consumer Psychology 16(2), 112-123 (typefaces measured on Osgood's evaluation, potency, activity)
Ou, Luo, Woodcock & Wright (2004), Color Research & Application 29(3) (colour emotion: three factors, colour activity, colour weight, colour heat)

findings.claim: The brain expects certain features to go together across senses and media (roundness with softness and sweetness, angularity with hardness), and binds congruent features more easily.
findings.use: Shape, type and motion of one piece agree on roundness; a soft drawing with a hard grotesque and a mechanical motion reads as three things.
sources: Spence (2011), Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 73, 971-995
Velasco, Woods, Hyndman & Spence (2015), i-Perception 6(4) (rounder typefaces matched to sweet, liked more and judged easier to read)

findings.claim: A typeface fits a product when they match on potency and activity; brands set in an appropriate font were chosen about twice as often.
findings.use: The pairing is chosen by its distance to the product's potency and activity first.
findings.strength: strong (two papers, forced-choice and rating studies)
sources: Doyle & Bottomley (2004), Journal of Business Research 57(8), 873-880 (font appropriateness and brand choice)
Doyle & Bottomley (2006), Journal of Consumer Psychology 16(2), 112-123

findings.claim: Typeface impressions come from a few design dimensions (elaborate, harmony, natural, flourish, weight, compressed) and trade off against each other (pleasing, engaging, reassuring, prominent).
findings.use: Pairings are profiled from their classification: weight and compression raise potency and activity; natural and flourish raise the hand axis; harmony (rounded, even strokes) raises roundness.
sources: Henderson, Giese & Cote (2004), Journal of Marketing 68(4), 60-72

findings.claim: Rounded shapes carry harmony and compromise; angular shapes carry confrontation and strength. People also prefer curved over sharp contours on average.
findings.use: Roundness of the style's drawing and corners follows the product's character: warm, caring, social products go round; competitive, technical, assertive ones may go angular.
sources: Zhang, Feick & Price (2006), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 32(6), 794-805
Bar & Neta (2006), Psychological Science 17(8), 645-648

findings.claim: Brightness and saturation, more than hue, drive emotional response: pleasure = .69 brightness + .22 saturation, arousal = -.31 brightness + .60 saturation, dominance = -.76 brightness + .32 saturation (standardised).
findings.use: Each Wada colour gets activity (arousal) and potency (dominance) from its lightness and chroma with these weights; a palette is the area-weighted mix of its colours.
findings.strength: strong (classic study, effects consistent for chromatic and achromatic colours; later replications agree on direction)
sources: Valdez & Mehrabian (1994), Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 123(4), 394-409
Wilms & Oberfeld (2018), Psychological Research 82, 896-914

findings.claim: Warm-cool is one of three colour-emotion factors that hold across cultures; reds, oranges and yellows read warm, blues and blue-greens cool, and the effect grows with chroma.
findings.use: Each colour's warmth is its chroma times its closeness to the warm hue direction (an approximation of the factor's direction; the published coefficients are not used here).
findings.strength: strong for the factor; the formula here is an approximation
sources: Ou, Luo, Woodcock & Wright (2004), Color Research & Application 29(3), 232-240 (Part I; Parts II and III in the same volume)
Ou et al. (2012), Color Research & Application 37(1) (eight countries: warm/cool, heavy/light and active/passive consistent across cultures)

findings.claim: Colour pairs are preferred and judged harmonious when their hues are similar; preference also rises with lightness contrast. But a figure colour is liked more the more its hue contrasts with the ground.
findings.use: Ground and text: similar hue, strong lightness contrast. Accent (the figure): hue contrast with the ground.
sources: Schloss & Palmer (2011), Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 73(2), 551-571

findings.claim: On average people like colours of things they like (clear-sky blues, clean water) and dislike colours of things they dislike (browns and dark yellows, olives: rot and waste).
findings.use: Dark yellow, olive and brown grounds are marked down unless the brand already owns that colour (brand meaning overrides the average).
findings.strength: strong for the average; individual and brand associations override it
sources: Palmer & Schloss (2010), PNAS 107(19), 8877-8882
Ou et al. (2004) Part III (least preferred colour near L*50, a*-8, b*30)

findings.claim: Colours fit a brand when their meaning matches its positioning (functional products in functional colours, sensory-social products in sensory-social colours); hue shifts brand personality (red excitement, blue competence) and saturation and brightness strengthen it.
findings.use: The palette is scored against the product's own warmth and activity, and against the colours people already know the brand by.
sources: Bottomley & Doyle (2006), Marketing Theory 6(1), 63-84
Labrecque & Milne (2012), Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 40(5), 711-727

findings.claim: Things that are easy to process are liked more: congruent, familiar and simple combinations feel right before anyone can say why.
findings.use: Components that agree (congruence) and colours close to the brand's known colours (familiarity) are scored up.
sources: Reber, Schwarz & Winkielman (2004), Personality and Social Psychology Review 8(4), 364-382

findings.claim: A moderately incongruent element is evaluated better than a fully congruent or extremely incongruent one: it invites a small act of discovery that resolves. Extreme incongruity frustrates.
findings.use: Exactly one deliberate tension per combination (one axis where one component differs moderately), never several.
findings.strength: moderate (well cited; method questioned in later work)
sources: Mandler (1982), in Clark & Fiske (eds), Affect and Cognition
Meyers-Levy & Tybout (1989), Journal of Consumer Research 16(1), 39-54

findings.claim: Design complexity (an elaborate, creative arrangement) increases attention and liking; feature complexity (dense edges, clutter, colour variation) decreases attention to the brand and liking.
findings.use: Busy styles are chosen only for high-activity products and still keep text zones calm; calm products get calm styles.
sources: Pieters, Wedel & Batra (2010), Journal of Marketing 74(5), 48-60

findings.claim: Picture motion raises arousal (physiologically and in self-report), more so when the image is already arousing, and intensifies its valence.
findings.use: Motion amount follows the product's activity: calm products get one slow movement or none; energetic products may move more, still one thing at a time.
sources: Detenber, Simons & Bennett (1998), Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media 42(1), 113-127

findings.claim: Handwritten type makes people feel a person was there; machine type reads as clearer and more credible.
findings.use: The hand axis decides whether a hand face is used at all; facts, numbers and buttons stay in type (foundations/research/handwriting.json).
sources: Schroll, Schnurr & Grewal (2018), Journal of Marketing Research 55(5)
Song & Schwarz (2008), Psychological Science 19(10)

findings.claim: Unity and variety both raise aesthetic appreciation while suppressing each other; designs that balance them are preferred, and unity is the dominant factor that makes variety enjoyable.
findings.use: General liking scores unity (components agreeing) first and adds a smaller reward for one controlled variation (the accent's hue contrast, one moderate tension).
sources: Post, Blijlevens & Hekkert (2016), Acta Psychologica 163, 142-152

findings.claim: Most advanced, yet acceptable: typicality and novelty jointly predict preference while suppressing each other; the best designs keep a recognisable structure and add something new.
findings.use: Recipes stay within a style's typical choices (its recommended palettes and core pairings) and allow one novel element.
sources: Hekkert, Snelders & van Wieringen (2003), British Journal of Psychology 94, 111-124

findings.claim: People prefer curved over angular contours, across cultures (Mexico, Ghana, Spain) and to a smaller degree in other primates; the preference seems to be for curves themselves rather than fear of angles.
findings.use: A small general-liking bonus for rounder combinations; angular combinations stay for moods that need strength or precision.
findings.strength: strong for the preference; the explanation is debated
sources: Bar & Neta (2006), Psychological Science 17(8), 645-648
Gómez-Puerto, Munar & Nadal (2016), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 9, 712
Palumbo, Ruta & Bertamini (2015), PLOS ONE (curvature preferred, not angularity avoided)

findings.claim: Higher figure-ground contrast makes things easier to see and they are judged prettier; symmetry, contrast and clarity work through the same processing fluency.
findings.use: Text contrast counts for liking, not only for access: more contrast scores higher, with diminishing returns.
sources: Reber, Winkielman & Schwarz (1998), Psychological Science 9, 45-48
Reber, Schwarz & Winkielman (2004), Personality and Social Psychology Review 8(4), 364-382

findings.claim: Blue is the most consistently preferred hue across studies and cultures; brighter, moderately saturated colours are liked more than dark, muddy ones.
findings.use: A small bonus for palettes with a clear blue; colour pleasure (brightness and saturation) counts for general liking.
findings.strength: strong for the average; context and brand override it
sources: Hurlbert & Ling (2007), Current Biology 17(16), R623-R625
Palmer & Schloss (2010), PNAS 107(19)
Valdez & Mehrabian (1994)

findings.claim: How liking follows complexity depends on the kind of complexity: Berlyne's inverted U (moderate is best) holds for some dimensions and not others; liking is often linear while beauty peaks in the middle.
findings.use: No blanket rule for 'more' or 'less': busy styles are kept to moods that want energy, and feature clutter is avoided everywhere (Pieters et al.).
findings.strength: moderate (mixed findings, explained by different complexity dimensions)
sources: Berlyne (1971), Aesthetics and Psychobiology
Nadal, Munar, Marty & Cela-Conde (2010), Empirical Studies of the Arts 28(2), 173-191

myths.claim: Each colour has one fixed meaning (red = danger, blue = trust).
myths.reality: Meaning depends on context, product and culture; brightness and saturation carry more of the emotion than hue (Valdez & Mehrabian 1994; Labrecque & Milne 2012).

myths.claim: Pick the best colour, the best font and the best style separately and the result is best.
myths.reality: Fit between components is what is judged (Doyle & Bottomley 2006; Spence 2011): three good parts that disagree read worse than three plain parts that agree.
One moderate, resolvable surprise beats total predictability (Meyers-Levy & Tybout 1989); several surprises read as noise.
